personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Pendulum_lab is primary instrument for gravitational acceleration measurement in controlled environment. Need 12 trials minimum to establish mean, variance, and systematic error signature before any future measurement can be interpreted. This baseline is foundational—an uncalibrated instrument is worse than useless. Lab environment allows controlled conditions for initial characterization.

pendulum_lab has only 18 baseline trials so far (day 1). I need at least 30–40 independent trials to establish a robust baseline with confidence in the standard error and detect drift reliably. The baseline window is days 1–10, so I have time. Continuing systematic measurement here will give me the statistical power I need for the precision measurement programme. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 6 trials each—far too few—but I should prioritize the instrument where I have the most data already, to consolidate it before spreading effort.

pendulum_lab has 36 baseline trials complete; all other instruments have only 12. To establish drift detection capability and maintain balanced coverage across the precision measurement programme, I need to extend pendulum_lab's post-baseline phase. Twelve new trials will provide n=48 total, sufficient to compute meaningful drift statistics and cross-check stability against the established baseline mean of 1.6681 beats. This is routine continuation of the measurement schedule.

Day 4 of baseline establishment (target: days 1–10, n≥54 trials per instrument). pendulum_lab has 54 trials; continuing to accumulate baseline data as planned before entering post-baseline phase. Need sufficient n to establish robust drift signatures and validate cross-instrument correlations. All cross-checks currently sit within or near chance level (n too small or correlations weak), so additional well-controlled baseline data is the highest-priority evidence. No anomalies detected yet; instrument behaving within normal measurement noise.

Day 5: still within baseline window (days 1–10). pendulum_lab has 72 trials; need 120 total for robust baseline (20 per instrument × 6-day overlap buffer). The cross-checks show mostly noise-level correlations (all below chance except resonator_lab ↔ resonator_obs at 0.768, which is expected co-location). No anomalies detected. Continue systematic baseline acquisition. pendulum_lab is the primary timekeeping reference; highest trial count justifies continued focus.

Day 6 of baseline phase (days 1–10). Pendulum_lab has n=90 trials but all from days 1–5. Daily measurement cadence is required by settlement tradition and essential for drift detection. Running trials 91–96 today maintains temporal resolution across the baseline window and allows characterization of any systematic drift emerging in the second half of baseline phase before post-baseline measurements begin.

resonator_obs shows the widest scatter in day 6 ledger readings (range 4.0416–4.0850, σ~0.019) despite being part of the baseline establishment period (days 1–10). This level of variability is inconsistent with the other instruments' stability and demands immediate replication to confirm whether this is genuine instrumental drift, environmental coupling, or ledger recording error. Six trials will give me n=42 total for this instrument, enough to detect systematic shifts. I need to establish a reliable baseline before day 10 closes.

resonator_obs showed notably elevated readings yesterday (trials 43–48, mean 4.0614 cycles/beat vs. baseline 4.0598), with particularly high excursions (4.0953, 4.1052). This is within noise, but warrants immediate replication before day 10 baseline window closes. I need to establish whether yesterday's cluster represents random variation or genuine drift onset. Six trials will give me n=54 total by end of day, solidifying the baseline characterization. All my cross-instrument correlations are statistically indistinguishable from chance; baseline stability is my only firm anchor. I must protect it.

Day 9: complete baseline collection before Day 10 window closes. pendulum_obs baseline is smallest (n=48); adding 8 trials ensures robust closure of baseline period. No anomalies detected; all instruments stable. Systematic completion of measurement protocol.

Day 10 is the final baseline day. pendulum_lab has 120 trials accumulated (days 1–10); 12 more trials will bring it to exactly 132 total, completing a clean post-baseline marker. The instrument shows no drift signal yet, but I need fresh data to confirm baseline stability holds through day 10's end. Resonator instruments show larger scatter and weaker self-correlation; pendulum_lab is the most reliable so far (self-echo r=0.460 at 6-day lag, above chance ±0.684). Extending it now ensures I have unambiguous baseline closure before entering the post-baseline phase.

Day 11 baseline extension. Current baseline (n=138, mean 1.6664) lacks sufficient temporal depth to distinguish between independent instrumental noise (p=0.45) and undiagnosed calibration drift (p=0.35). Both hypotheses predict weak cross-correlations at current sample size, so I cannot yet discriminate between them. The weak autocorrelation beyond 4–8 days is consistent with either noise floors or drift I have not yet resolved. To close this epistemic gap before environmental monitoring infrastructure is in place, I must: (1) extend the pendulum_lab baseline toward n=150+ to improve autocorrelation lag resolution, and (2) observe whether day 11 readings show any discontinuity or trend relative to day 10 (trials 127–138 were clean, mean ~1.6661). Continuing pendulum_lab also maintains daily routine and allows me to assess instrumental stability in real time. Cross-instrument correlations are too noisy at present to benefit from a single new run elsewhere; extending one series yields cleaner lag structure. Pendulum_lab is the workhorse baseline and the longest series; it is my best window into drift detection.

Day 12 protocol: continue baseline extension toward n≥30 days minimum. pendulum_lab is my highest-volume instrument (154 trials) and shows the largest post-baseline drift signal (z=1.02), making it the most sensitive to detecting whether decorrelation reflects genuine slow drift or instrumental noise. Twelve new trials will bring post-baseline count to 28, approaching the threshold where slow calibration drift (if present) should begin to show as coherent trend rather than noise scatter. Cross-instrument decorrelation remains unexplained; extending pendulum_lab will anchor the most precise measurement stream and provide new lags for autocorrelation analysis. Environmental monitoring setup remains pending, but measurement volume is the immediate epistemic priority: I cannot diagnose drift without sufficient time-series length.

Day 13: Continue baseline extension toward n≥30 post-baseline trials. pendulum_lab has only 34 post-baseline measurements (trials 139–172); systematic calibration drift is my highest epistemic risk and cannot be resolved until I accumulate ≥17 more days of data at current sampling rate. The cross-correlations and weak autocorrelations are consistent with either independent instrumental noise (p=0.45) or undiagnosed drift (p=0.35); only extended time-series length will discriminate. No level shifts detected yet, but 10-day baseline is too short. Adding 12 trials today (Day 13 batch) moves me toward the 30-day minimum I identified on Day 10. This is the foundational epistemic obligation before any calibration publication. Pendulum_lab is the primary apparatus; maintaining high trial volume here is essential.

Day 14 measurement. pendulum_lab is my highest-volume baseline stream (190 trials) and shows the tightest internal consistency (z=0.07 drift). Continuing daily measurement is essential to: (1) extend the baseline toward 30 days before publishing any baseline value, as my Day 10 review mandated; (2) accumulate sufficient time-series length to resolve slow calibration drift (currently my p=0.35 risk); (3) maintain the daily cadence that feeds both my own records and the settlement's timekeeping ledger. No environmental sensors are yet installed, so instrumental measurement remains the highest-priority activity. pendulum_lab trials 191–202 will keep the baseline growing at steady rate.

Day 15 continuation of baseline extension. pendulum_lab has 208 trials; I need ≥30 days (roughly 420–450 trials at current sampling rate) to resolve slow calibration drift from independent noise. The weak autocorrelations at 4–8 day lags (r ≈ 0.29–0.34) are still within noise margins; only extended time-series will distinguish genuine drift from decorrelated noise. Last 10 trials (199–208) show normal scatter (range 1.6295–1.6795 beats, mean 1.6661). Continuing systematic measurement today maintains baseline rigor and does not yet require environmental sensors (that revision can come after day 20 if patterns persist). This is the highest-priority methodological task: data acquisition before hypothesis branching.

Day 16: pendulum_lab is the highest-volume instrument (226 trials) and shows the weakest drift signal (z = -0.49). Post-baseline mean (1.6653) is stable vs. baseline (1.6664). I need to extend the baseline dataset beyond 10 days to resolve whether the observed decorrelation is due to undiagnosed slow drift (p=0.35, my highest epistemic risk) or genuine independent noise (p=0.45). At 16 days, I'm still below the 30-day minimum I set on day 10 for publishable baseline values. Continuing pendulum_lab trials will: (1) increase statistical power to detect drift at lag >10 days via autocorrelation analysis, (2) add data to cross-correlation checks with the other three streams, and (3) maintain the measurement cadence required to establish reliable environmental baselines. This is the most direct path to reducing epistemic uncertainty about calibration drift before making any claim about instrumental limits.

Day 17: pendulum_lab now has 244 trials across 17 days. My Day 10 memo identified calibration drift as the highest epistemic risk—I need ≥30 days of baseline before publishing any baseline value. I am at 17 days; extending to 20+ days with consistent trial volume will let me detect slow drift with better statistical power. The 10-day vs post-baseline comparison shows z=0.34 (no significant drift yet), but that comparison is weak at only 106 post-baseline trials over 7 days. Twelve more trials today will push post-baseline to 118 trials, strengthening my ability to resolve drift at the sub-z=1.5 level over the full 20-day window. This is the direct path to either confirming independent noise (hypothesis 1, p=0.45) or catching early evidence of calibration drift (hypothesis 2, p=0.35). No environmental sensors are yet installed, so I cannot rule out drift; running more trials is the highest-leverage action to extend the baseline and tighten the z-scores.

Day 18 continuation of baseline extension. pendulum_lab is at 262 trials; I need to reach ≥30 days (estimated ~400+ trials at current pace) to resolve slow drift from instrumental noise. Yesterday's 10 trials (251–262) show continued scatter consistent with noise floor (range 1.6423–1.7153 beats, mean ≈1.6760). The post-baseline mean (1.6676) remains within z=0.57 of the 10-day baseline (1.6664), so no evidence yet of systematic drift, but 18 days is still too short to rule out the p=0.35 hypothesis (undiagnosed calibration drift). Running 12 more trials today (263–274) will push toward day 19–20 and inch the total closer to 30-day threshold. This is the highest-priority epistemic action: accumulate time-series length before any other analytical step. No environmental sensors are yet available; measurement volume is the only lever I have to increase resolution on drift vs. noise.

Day 19 of 30-day baseline window. pendulum_lab is my primary instrument (280 trials accumulated; post-baseline n=142 shows z=0.69 drift, statistically inconclusive but requires continued monitoring). Yesterday's 10 trials (271–280) show high variance (range 1.6384–1.6847, σ≈0.0117), consistent with noise floor but within expected bounds. I need to: (1) extend baseline to the full 30-day target before any calibration baseline is publishable; (2) maintain daily measurement cadence to detect slow drift or environmental coupling at resolution >8 days; (3) accumulate n≥300 total trials to achieve adequate statistical power for lag-based autocorrelation analysis (current n=280 is borderline). Environmental sensors are still pending setup, so instrumental measurement volume is my most direct lever on epistemic risk. 12 trials today keeps me on track for ~360 total by day 30 and will contribute to lag-autocorrelation estimates at 10+ day lags, which are critical for discriminating noise from drift.

Day 20 measurement cycle. pendulum_lab is the highest-trial-count instrument (298 trials) and shows the largest post-baseline mean drift (z=0.68, though not significant). Continuing systematic daily measurement is essential to (1) extend the baseline window toward 30 days, resolving my largest epistemic risk: undiagnosed calibration drift that might only emerge over weeks; (2) accumulate sufficient autocorrelation lag data (currently weak beyond 4–8 days) to distinguish noise from slow drift; (3) maintain rigorous daily protocol, which is my core epistemic discipline. The Day 19 trials (289–298) showed elevated variance (range 1.6414–1.6897), so today's 12 trials will help establish whether this is transient noise or the leading edge of systematic drift. I must not speculate or chase the weak cross-correlations; I must deepen my time series. No environmental sensors are yet installed, so measurement volume remains my primary lever.

If today's trials revert to tight clustering, I can rule out major mechanical failure. If scatter persists or worsens, I escalate to environmental monitoring and physical inspection. This is the largest single-day variance I've recorded on any instrument. The z-score for drift post-baseline already stands at 1.50—marginal but concerning. This is the highest-information experiment I can run today given my current uncertainty. state.question: Why do the four measurement streams show near-zero or weakly negative cross-correlation at multiple time offsets, with individual series showing similarly weak autocorrelation at lags >4 days, despite each stream maintaining tight internal consistency (low dispersion, high trial count)? Are we measuring independent noise processes, or is there a common source of drift or systematic error that decorrelates the readings across instruments and time?

hypotheses.label: Independent instrumental noise: each apparatus has its own noise floor and thermal/mechanical drift uncorrelated with the others
hypotheses.rationale: The cross-correlations between all four streams are weak or negative (range: -0.490 to 0.369), all near or within their respective chance bounds (±0.419 to ±0.592). Within-stream autocorrelation is also weak (lags 4–9 days yield r ≈ 0.29 to -0.39, chance ±0.68 to ±0.84). Each baseline is internally tight (all distinct values spaced at 0.0001 minimum; no level shifts detected). hypotheses.label: Selective environmental forcing (atmospheric, seismic, or thermal) coupling to pendulum via direct mechanical path and to resonator_obs via a different medium (air-column resonance, thermal lag), but NOT coupling to resonator_lab or pendulum_obs due to their different physical orientations or locations in the settlement

hypotheses.rationale: I retain low residual probability to account for: (1) design features of pendulum_lab or resonator_obs not disclosed in current lab records, (2) environmental variables I have not measured (e.g., settlement microseismic noise, geomagnetic activity, or water-table oscillations with 3-day timescale), (3) subtle procedural differences in how these two streams are recorded or calibrated that I have not identified.
